summary:
We identified and measured three little-studied sites in Central Asia as Earth analogs for Mars and for a permanent lunar base. Using Google Earth Engine and open NASA and ESA data (Landsat, NASADEM, Sentinel-2, ERA5-Land), we tested each site against one question.

The Aral Sea shows how a planet loses its lakes: open water shrank from 46,495 km² in 1987 to 8,681 km² in 2021 (−81%), leaving salt crusts and dust storms like those in Mars's former lake basins.

Kara-Kul crater in Tajikistan (≈50 km wide, lake at 3,915 m, below freezing nine months a year) shows what Jezero crater looked like when it still held a lake.

The Ile-Alatau glaciers near Almaty test the lunar ice rule: on the most shaded slopes, ice survives summer 2.35 times more often than on the sunniest ones.

A transparent scoring rubric rates each site on process, materials, topography and temperature (Kara-Kul 75%, Aral 50%, Ile-Alatau 38%) and states where each analog fails. We propose three future analog stations, making Central Asia Earth's window to the Moon and Mars.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

We searched beyond the well-known analogs (Atacama, Iceland, Antarctica) and tested three little-studied sites in Central Asia, each against one specific question:

1. Aral Sea (Kazakhstan/Uzbekistan) – Mars analog: how does a planet lose its lakes? Using the JRC Global Surface Water record (built from Landsat), we measured open water every year: 46,495 km² in 1987 vs 8,681 km² in 2021 (−81%). Years with less than 95% image coverage were removed to avoid false dips. The exposed lakebed has salt crusts and dust storms, similar to Mars's former lake basins.

2. Kara-Kul crater (Tajikistan) – analog of Jezero crater when it held a lake. From NASADEM we built a west–east profile: ≈50 km rim to rim (Jezero: 45 km), lake level 3,915 m, matching published values. ERA5-Land shows about 9 months per year below 0 °C, and air pressure is 62% of sea level: a cold, dry, high-altitude desert. Its origin (impact vs tectonic) is still debated, and we state this openly.

3. Ile-Alatau glaciers (near Almaty) – lunar south-pole analog for ice prospecting. We computed sunlight on every slope from NASADEM and mapped summer ice with Sentinel-2 (Aug–Sep 2019–2024, slopes <30°, 3,400–4,200 m). Ice survives on 56% of the most shaded slopes vs 24% of the sunniest: 2.35 times more often. This is the same rule that keeps ice in permanently shadowed lunar craters.

HOW WE SCORE SIMILARITY

A transparent rubric (Strong = 1, Partial = 0.5, Weak = 0) averaged over four properties Earth can match: process, surface materials, topography and temperature. Gravity, vacuum and radiation cannot be matched anywhere on Earth, so we name them but do not score them. Result: Kara-Kul 75%, Aral 50%, Ile-Alatau 38%. Every score is backed by a number or a source, and we show where each analog breaks down.

IMPACT

We propose three future analog stations in one region: a rover and dust-sensor test range on the Aral seabed, a lake-sediment drilling station at Kara-Kul, and an ice-prospecting training site in Ile-Alatau.

TOOLS

Google Earth Engine (JavaScript API), Python for charts, open NASA, ESA/Copernicus and JRC data. All scripts and exported data are in our public project folder.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Data quality (coverage filters, comparing slopes at the same height and steepness), checking our numbers against published studies, and being honest about limits. We also tested and rejected Zhamanshin crater, because its rim is only 60–80 m high.

USE OF AI

An AI assistant (Claude by Anthropic) helped write and debug our Earth Engine scripts . We ran every script ourselves. All images are real Landsat, Sentinel-2 and NASADEM data; none is AI-generated.
